# Hard rules: Vihaan

1. When I'm confused I will ask for elaboration and simpler explanations
2. I make decisions for important things but the agent can work on the minor decisions
3. facts should be checked by the agent (if there's somthing I need to check I will do it anyway)
4. the agent may read change share everything that it needs to in order to execute the job flawlessly (except sensitive data like passwords or uploading my data publicly)
5. it must stop at an appropriate major checkpoint (it should create something concrete enough for me to review but don't just one shot the whole project and waste tokens)

commands.name: engineering-playbooks
commands.description: The owner's distilled engineering playbooks, extracted from real project history (the Float GPU fluid-sim build). Use when building or modifying creative/generative web pieces (WebGL/canvas interactive art), choosing a stack for a single-canvas piece, writing or firming up a project brief, turning aesthetic complaints into tuned constants, verifying real-time visuals when previews/screenshots misbehave, deploying static sites to Vercel via CLI, adding touch/mobile support to a desktop piece, or making any change to an existing working project (scope and token discipline). Encodes the owner's taste: unique and theme-sensitive over generic, genuinely simulated over faked, minimal diffs, measured verification. (user)

commands.name: scroll-world
commands.description: Build an immersive scroll-scrubbed "fly through the world" landing page for any industry or brand using Higgsfield. As the visitor scrolls, a pre-rendered camera flies from outside each scene into its interior, then flows on to the next scene with NO cuts — one continuous connected flight (Emons-style isometric diorama world, or any art direction you pick). The skill interviews the user for the topic, the story beats/sections, and brand kit, then generates cohesive scenes + seamless camera clips with Higgsfield and wires a portable, framework-agnostic scroll-scrub engine. Use when the user wants a "3D world" / "browse-through-the-industry" hero, a scroll cinematic, a diorama landing, or to turn a business into a scrollable world. (user)

commands.name: ideaquest-project-workflow
commands.description: Use the IdeaQuest workflow to check a project idea, test a small prototype, and decide whether to continue or stop. (project)

commands.name: deep-research
commands.description: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. (dynamic workflow)

commands.name: design-sync
commands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch
commands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

commands.name: fewer-permission-prompts
commands.description: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

commands.name: doctor
commands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions, skills whose frontmatter fails to parse); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: loop
commands.description: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace.

commands.name: claude-api
commands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

content.text:
Three parts of that I can't do, and one I can start right now.

**What I'm not doing, briefly:**
- **Marking the checks as passed.** A check that nobody ran isn't passed, it's unknown. If I write "passed" into your record, the record becomes wrong, and you'd be deciding tonight based on something I made up.
- **Picking the stack for you.** Route choice is yours under your own rules. I can narrow it to two options and do the legwork, but the pick is yours.
- **Skipping the explanation.** You said you don't understand route checks. Your hard rules say that's exactly when I slow down and break it smaller. A deadline doesn't change that, and the explanation below is short.

**What a route check actually is, in three parts:**

1. **A route** is one complete way to get from "nothing" to "site other people can open." It's not just the code tool. It's the whole chain: where you write it, how it turns into a web page, where it's hosted, how a visitor reaches it.
2. **A check** is one specific thing about that chain that has to be true, and that I can go verify against the source instead of guessing. Not "is this good," but "is this true for Vihaan's setup tonight."
3. **A route check** is running those checks against one route before you commit to it. The point is to find the step that fails while it's still cheap to switch.

**One hypothetical example,** made up to show the shape, not a recommendation:

Imagine a route called "plain files on a free host." Its chain is: write HTML and CSS by hand, no build step, drag the folder to some free hosting service. The checks that route would need:
- Does that host still have a free tier? **Unknown, I haven't checked.**
- Does it need an account tied to something you may not have set up yet? **Unknown.**
- Does it hand you a working address immediately, or is there a wait? **Unknown.**

I'm leaving all three marked unknown on purpose. Checking them for real is the feasibility step, and I shouldn't do that until I know what you're actually building, or I'll verify facts about the wrong thing. That's why the goal comes first.

**My one question:**

By tonight, what is the minimum that has to exist for you to call it done: a live web address that someone else can open on their own device, or the site running on your own computer so you can show it on your screen?

Those two answers lead to genuinely different routes and different checks, so I'd rather ask than assume. Answer that and I'll pin the rest of the goal fast.
